verdicts.strongest_argument: Every underlying fact checks out, and I concede the mechanism lands squarely inside this print's window (BizLink May+Jun+Jul maps almost exactly onto Credo's fiscal Q1, 3 May - 1 Aug 2026). But the finding is a read-across inference, and both halves of that inference are weaker than stated. First, the arithmetic: the hunter compares a May-to-July month-over-month chain (9,630/7,352 = +31.0%) against a quarter-over-quarter revenue guide. The like-for-like comparison against Credo's fiscal quarters is BizLink Feb+Mar+Apr = NT$20,784.6m versus May+Jun+Jul = NT$25,500.4m, i.e. +22.7% QoQ, and February is Chinese-New-Year-depressed (-14.3% MoM), which flatters the base; normalising February to trend puts it near +19%. So the claimed gap versus the +6.4%/+8.7% guide is overstated by roughly a third. Second, attribution: BizLink's own Q2 call on 2026-08-21 attributes the growth to HPC (+67% YoY, 42% of mix) and Capital Equipment (+52% YoY) and makes no mention of AEC, Credo or any specific customer. BizLink Holding runs at roughly NT$95bn annualised (Jan-Jul 2026 cumulative NT$53.74bn); Credo's entire AEC cost of goods paid to its contract manufacturers is on the order of US$200-300m/yr, so Credo is plausibly 7-8% of BizLink's consolidated revenue, and BizLink also serves NVIDIA rack-scale copper directly while Credo also uses Foxlink as a secondary manufacturer. A 22.7% move in the aggregate says very little about a 7-8% slice. Third, on publication: the monthly figures are TWSE-mandated disclosures and were reported contemporaneously by cnyes for May (June 2026) and June (July 2026), and BizLink is one of the most closely followed Taiwan AI-supply-chain names, so the data itself is public and monitored by every Asia tech desk. What I could NOT find, after repeated searching, is any article drawing the BizLink-to-Credo read-across, and the tape supports that: CRDO's 20-day run-up is -1.19% across the window containing the July monthly print (~5-10 Aug), so nothing was bid on this. That combination -- published and reported, not obviously connected to this print, magnitude genuinely contested -- is the 45-65 band, and I place it at the bottom of it because the US-facing connection is absent. I accept the fact and reject the size, not the sign.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Run-up 20d of -1.19% and 5d of -3.08% spans the 5-10 August window in which the record July monthly revenue became public, and CRDO did not rally on it, so this is not visibly in the price. The 25-delta skew of +7.31 vol points and the stock sitting -28.68% from its 52-week high indicate the market's paid-for worry is margin and customer concentration, not revenue -- so a revenue-upside signal is orthogonal to the priced lean rather than a restatement of it. Against that, consensus revenue of $470.7-471.7m sits at the midpoint-to-high-end of the $465-475m guide, and Zacks records an average EPS surprise of 27.4% over the trailing four quarters, so a beat per se is already the base case; only a beat materially above the routine is information.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A disclosed Credo share of BizLink revenue above ~20%, or a published sell-side note or Taiwan trade piece explicitly making the BizLink-to-Credo Q1 read-across, would move this in opposite directions -- the former down to ~25, the latter up to ~70.

verdicts.strongest_argument: I verified the absence directly and it is factually correct: Credo's last 8-K of any kind is 2026-06-01 (accession 0001628280-26-039474), and the complete filing record from 2026-06-01 to today contains only Forms 4, 144s, the 10-K of 2026-06-15, a 13G/A, the DEF 14A and ARS of 2026-08-25 and an SD. No Item 2.02, nothing. So the fact stands. The inference does not carry the weight placed on it, for three separate reasons, and what remains is priced. (1) Observability: EDGAR is free, real-time and universally monitored, and the equivalent-calendar deadline for a pre-announcement passed around 10 August (nine days after the 1 August quarter end, matching the Feb-9-after-Jan-31 precedent). Every analyst covering the name has had three weeks to observe that nothing came. An absence that any reader can confirm in ten seconds is the definition of structurally known. (2) Base rate: Credo has been public since January 2022 and has pre-announced preliminary revenue exactly once in roughly eighteen quarters -- in the single most extreme quarter of its history, when revenue grew 51.9% sequentially and beat guidance by ~19%. The absence of a pre-announcement is therefore the modal outcome, and its entire information content is 'there is no 19%-scale blowout', which a consensus pinned at the guide midpoint ($470.7m against a $465-475m guide) already assumes. (3) The price history runs the wrong way for the implied sign: the one quarter Credo did pre-announce (+9.16% on 2026-02-09) was followed twenty-one days later by the worst reaction in the whole sample (-14.81% on 2026-03-02), while the two most recent quarters with no pre-announcement printed +1.28% and +7.40%. So 'no pre-announcement' has no demonstrated bearish signature in this name's own reaction record. I take the brief's point seriously that an absence is unfalsifiable in a way a positive disclosure is not: if Credo beats hard tonight, nothing in this finding can be shown to have been wrong, and that asymmetry is exactly why it should not be sized as though it were a disclosure.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The absence became knowable around 10 August; the 20-day run-up is -1.19% and the 5-day is -3.08%, with the stock -28.68% from its 52-week high and puts bid at +7.31 vol points of 25-delta skew. That is a tape consistent with no positive catalyst having arrived and with the market not positioned for a blowout -- i.e. the absence is already reflected. Consensus at $470.7-471.7m against a $465-475m guide is the direct numerical evidence that nobody is modelling the Feb-2026-style upside whose absence this finding infers.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that a pre-announcement was widely expected this quarter -- a published note or a bid in September upside calls in the first half of August -- would make the absence genuine news and move this toward 35.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Every element of this finding is verified and every element is published guidance. The 2026-06-01 release gives Q1 FY27 revenue of $465-475m and non-GAAP gross margin of 67.0-69.0% against Q4 FY26 actual non-GAAP GM of 68.3%; the call confirms 'mid single digit sequential growth in the first half', the CFO's 'similar in our Q2 guide when that comes', and FY27 non-GAAP gross margin 'to be broadly consistent with fiscal year 2026 levels' (FY26 was 68.1%). That is the top of the 90-100 band -- it restates published guidance, it is in the 8-K, the press release, the wire copy and every sell-side model, and consensus of $470.7-471.7m sits inside the guided range, which is the proof that the street has it. The attribution of the -14.81% on 2026-03-02 to the Q4 GM guide cut to 64-66% rather than to revenue is also correct, and was necessarily correct because the Feb 9 pre-announcement had already removed revenue as a surprise -- but that was extensively reported at the time and is not new. Separately from pricing, I reject the finding's logic, and this is a sign/inference rejection rather than a factual one. Guidance given in June is not a pre-commitment against a revision in September; it is precisely the thing that gets revised. The March 2026 episode is the counterexample inside the finding's own evidence: management had a standing gross-margin expectation and cut it, and the stock fell 14.81%. Saying the mechanisms were 'pre-committed' therefore removes no risk at all. And the +7.31 vol-point skew was set by a market that has had this guidance for three months -- so the skew is not mispricing the guidance, it is pricing the probability that the guidance changes. A claim that the skew is wrong because management already guided is an argument the option market has already heard and declined.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The skew of +7.31 vol points and the 9.6% event-implied move were set on 2026-09-01, three months after this guidance was public. A market paying up for downside in full knowledge of a reassuring 67-69% GM guide is not a market that has failed to read the guide; it is a market pricing revision risk, which the finding does not address. The -14.81% of 2026-03-02 is in the reaction history and is the single largest downside observation in the sample, so the mechanism the finding claims is de-risked is precisely the one the option market has evidence to fear.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Nothing short of showing the guidance was not in consensus; since consensus sits inside the guided range, that is closed off.

interactions: CRDO#0 and CRDO#1 are direct mirrors on one question -- is there a large revenue upside surprise in fiscal Q1 FY27 -- and they answer it oppositely. CRDO#0 infers from a supplier proxy that Credo is running roughly 20 points of sequential growth above a +6.4%/+8.7% guide; CRDO#1 observes that Credo, which pre-announced the last time it was blowing out that badly, said nothing this time. CRDO#1 is the better-quality evidence of the two, because it is the issuer's own behaviour rather than a 7-8%-weight third party's consolidated aggregate, and the Feb 2026 precedent shows Credo does disclose when the gap is that large. Taken together the pair should reduce confidence in CRDO#0's magnitude rather than add up, and a ranking that scores both as independent positives would be double-counting a contradiction. CRDO#1 and CRDO#2 rest on the same two events -- the 2026-02-09 pre-announcement and the 2026-03-02 margin-cut reaction -- and read them for different purposes without conflict. CRDO#2 and CRDO#0 also collide on a specific number: CRDO#2 treats the CFO's implied ~$490-500m Q2 guide as a floor that de-risks the print, while CRDO#0 implies that same guide is about to be left far behind; both cannot be the operative fact tonight. Finally, CRDO#2's premise cuts against itself -- it cites the March 2026 guidance cut as proof that margin is the crash mechanism while simultaneously arguing that a June margin guide prevents a September cut.
